titulo.texto: Water, Steam, and Color: The North Complex

frase_gancho.texto: Where a city on a hilltop worked out its water, its bodies, and its rituals.

puente_narrativo.texto: Continue your route: what comes next shows other spaces of the city.

guion_corto.texto: A city of between ten thousand and fifteen thousand people, high on a hill, had to solve the problem of water. According to the INAH, north of the plaza there is a cistern, part of the water system. Unknown Mexico describes it as a rainwater cistern, with drainage. The INAH guide includes here a temazcal, a steam bath with a ceremonial purpose, and the Hall of the Polychrome Altar, which helps us understand how roofs were built. Polychrome means painted in several colors. According to Andrews and Glascock, there were temazcals on the Acropolis and in this north sector. Check with the site staff to find out which is which. People lived here, worked here, and prayed here.

guion_largo.texto:
A city on a hilltop faces a problem that does not show up in photos: water.

According to Hirth, between ten thousand and fifteen thousand people came to live in Xochicalco. All of them needed to drink, cook, and work. The INAH mentions a cistern north of the plaza, part of the city’s water system. Unknown Mexico describes it as a rainwater cistern, with drainage. In other words, there was a way to collect the rain and to let the excess flow out.

Very close by, according to the INAH guide, stood the temazcal. A temazcal is a steam bath. The guide says it had a ceremonial purpose, meaning that it served to cleanse the body and also for ceremonies. According to Andrews and Glascock, there were temazcals in two places. One was on the Acropolis and the other in this north sector, next to the ball court. In that same sector they mention a large dam. If you see a small room with benches built against the walls, that may be it.

The third space is the Hall of the Polychrome Altar. Polychrome means painted in several colors. According to the INAH guide, this hall helps us understand how the roofs of the city were built. One source says that the reliefs of the Pyramid of the Feathered Serpents were painted red, green, yellow, blue, black, and white. Imagine color here too.

Water, steam, and color. Three things that in our lives are kept apart, and that here shared the same corner of the city.

When you walk through this complex, do not look for grand monuments. Look for the traces of daily life: where water was stored, where the body was cleansed, and where people prayed.
